artworkData.artworkName: The Bridge and Castel Sant’Angelo in Rome
artworkData.intro: Vernet’s sunlit view of Rome’s Tiber River sets a modest group of fishermen against a grand backdrop of classical architecture, including two monuments associated with the Emperor Hadrian. Whether depicting tranquil river landscapes or violent shipwrecks, Vernet’s marine paintings captivated eighteenth-century patrons who viewed them through the lens of their own colonial and maritime ambitions. By linking a humble contemporary scene of local commerce to the imperial splendor of ancient Rome, this painting may hint at how everyday maritime labor formed the bedrock of empires both past and present.

provenanceEvents.title: 1. Choiseul’s Classical and Colonial Visions
provenanceEvents.text:
Vernet painted this urban riverscape during the two decades he lived and worked in Rome, from the 1730s to the 1750s. Its first recorded owner was Étienne-François, duc de Choiseul (1719-89). Like Vernet, Choiseul also lived in Rome, where he served as Louis XV’s ambassador (1754-57) and developed a deep appreciation for ancient and neoclassical art. After returning to France, Choiseul became head of the navy and foreign ministry, alternating these positions with his cousin, the duc de Choiseul Praslin, during the 1760s. Their family had deep colonial ties that helped fund the impressive art collections both men assembled. It’s not known when Choiseul acquired this Vernet painting, or its pendant of another Roman bridge, but it was probably after his return to France. The two scenes likely evoked nostalgia for his time in Rome, while also appealing to a larger desire to model France’s commercial and maritime empire on ancient precedents.

Around this time, France suffered a damaging defeat in the Seven Years’ War (1756-63) that entailed the loss of Canada and other colonial territories. Choiseul subsequently launched a massive campaign to expand the French colony of Guiana. Propagandistic prints of Guiana were published to lure prospective colonists, some of which resembled Vernet’s idyllic maritime views, including a neoclassical scene of Bathers that Choiseul owned. The publicity scheme worked, and approximately 13,000 settlers—many of them migrant laborers from the war-torn Alsace and Rhine regions—were shipped to Guiana between 1763-65. However, Choiseul’s administration so badly mismanaged the project that the vast majority of them died.
provenanceEvents.imageSource: Giovanni Paolo Panini, Ancient Rome (detail with duc de Choiseul), 1757. Oil on canvas, 172.1 x 229.9 cm. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, Gwynne Andrews Fund, 1952.
provenanceEvents.imageAlt: Giovanni Paolo Panini, Ancient Rome (detail with duc de Choiseul), 1757.

provenanceEvents.title: 2. Art and Tea with the Prince de Conti
provenanceEvents.text:
After Choiseul, Vernet’s painting entered the collection of Louis François de Bourbon, prince de Conti (1717-76), the son-in-law of France’s former Regent. Conti speculated in colonial ventures and was a founding investor in the Société d’Affrique, a company that aimed to correct Choiseul’s mistakes and successfully expand the colony of Guiana by controlling land development and slave trading in the region. In 1777, the same year that a high-profile auction of Conti’s collection was held, the Société was renamed the French Guiana Company. Several of its investors acquired works in the sale, suggesting a deep entanglement between colonial speculation and art buying.

As Grand Prior of the Knights of Malta, Conti resided in Paris’s Palais du Temple, where he displayed his art collection and presided over a counter-court filled with Enlightenment luminaries such as Rousseau, Beaumarchais, and Diderot. In a painting of one these gatherings, the young Mozart plays the harpsichord while Conti’s guests consume tea and sugar—colonial products tied to systems of extraction and enslavement that made this rarefied world possible.
provenanceEvents.imageSource: Michel-Barthélémy Ollivier, Afternoon Tea at the Palais du Temple with the Entire Court of the Prince de Conti, 1766. Oil on canvas, 53 x 68 cm. Palace of Versailles. Image: Wikimedia Commons.
provenanceEvents.imageAlt: Michel-Barthélémy Ollivier, Afternoon Tea at the Palais du Temple with the Entire Court of the Prince de Conti, 1766.

provenanceEvents.title: 3. Colonial Filiations: The Rohan and Castelmore Families
provenanceEvents.text:
At Conti’s 1777 sale, Vernet’s Bridge passed into the hands of Louis-Antoine, duc de Rohan-Chabot (1733-1807), whose cousin, Louis-Armand-Constantin de Rohan, served as governor of Saint-Domingue after the Seven Years’ War. Rohan-Chabot sold the painting in 1787 to the comte de Castelmore (1787-1827), who also hailed from a colonial family: one of his ancestors had governed the French Antilles (from 1669-77) and was responsible for consolidating France’s hold over Martinique and expanding the slave trade there. Although neither collector was directly involved in colonial trade, their families played a major role in developing France’s two most significant Caribbean colonies, whose profits fueled the growth and splendor of eighteenth-century Paris.

Among the beneficiaries of this exploitative system were Parisian art dealers who had colonial collectors as their clients. Vernet’s Bridge was briefly owned by the dealers Feuillet and Paillet before they flipped the painting, selling it first to Rohan-Chabot and later to Simon-Charles Boutin. Together with Jean-Baptiste-Pierre Le Brun, these dealers helped create a huge market and inflated prices for Vernet’s work in the years preceding the French and Haitian Revolutions.
provenanceEvents.imageSource: Studio of Jean-Marc Nattier, Roch Aza et Louis-Armand-Constantin Rohan, Prince de Montbazon, 1758. Oil on canvas. © David Gallard / Château des ducs de Bretagne – Musée d’histoire de Nantes.
provenanceEvents.imageAlt: Studio of Jean-Marc Nattier, Roch Aza et Louis-Armand-Constantin Rohan, Prince de Montbazon, 1758.

provenanceEvents.title: 4. Plantations and Pleasure Gardens: Boutin’s Rendez-vous and Tivoli
provenanceEvents.text:
The last private owner of Vernet’s Bridge was the financier Simon-Charles Boutin (1719 -94), who acquired it in 1791. Boutin made his fortune through trade and planation speculation and served as France’s treasurer of the navy and the colonies. His taste for art collecting was instilled by his friend, the salonnière Madame Geoffrin, who left Boutin a large Vernet seascape in her will. Boutin was a noted supporter of neoclassical artists like Hubert Robert and Greuze, and in 1788 the artist Elisabeth Vigée Le Brun, wife of the art dealer Le Brun, threw a lavish Greek-inspired supper (the so-called souper grec) in honor of Boutin and another colonial collector, the comte de Vaudreuil. Many Paris art world elites attended, including Vernet’s daughter, the painter Émilie Chalgrin.

Around 1768, Boutin had built an elaborate park in Paris named Tivoli after the ancient site near Rome that many artists, including Vernet, visited. He opened Tivoli to the public and filled it with fragments of classical statues, a mineralogical cabinet, and specimens of flowers and birds obtained through colonial channels. Boutin also owned a large sugar plantation near Port au Prince in Saint-Domingue named “Rendezvous,” where 200 men, women, and children were listed as enslaved in a 1787-88 inventory. A rare surviving plan indicates that its main house, near the slave quarters, featured a French-style garden, the colonial counterpart to his jardin français at Tivoli. Boutin’s plantation profits supported his art buying, including the acquisition of Vernet’s Bridge and its pendant from the dealer Paillet in 1791—which, despite the upheavals of the French Revolution, was one of the most profitable years ever for Saint-Domingue planters and slave traders.
provenanceEvents.imageSource: Detail showing homes of enslaved workers on a plantation later acquired by Boutin. Plan de l'Habitation de Monsieur de La Porte-Lalanne, 1753. Ink and watercolor, 96 x 69 cm. William L. Clements Library, University of Michigan.
provenanceEvents.imageAlt: Detail showing homes of enslaved workers on a plantation later acquired by Boutin, 1753.

provenanceEvents.title: 5. The Beautiful and the Damned: Artworks Seized by Le Brun
provenanceEvents.text:
Vernet’s Bridge was seized along with the rest of Boutin’s art collection from his two Parisian residences (Tivoli and a hôtel on the rue de Richelieu) in September 1794. He had been arrested and guillotined that summer, due in part to his suspected friendship with Marie-Antoinette, a guest at Tivoli. Vigée Le Brun’s husband, who had joined the Revolutionary government’s new Commission des Arts—an organization in charge of seizing and nationalizing the property of condemned and emigrated aristocrats—went to Boutin’s home to draw up a detailed list of his possessions. He brought the painter Jean-Honoré Fragonard along to assist in this work.

Having been the primary dealer for many of these aristocrats, Le Brun was well aware of the artworks they owned and their value. Beginning with a bust of Hadrian “after the antique,” he carefully listed all the ancient sarcophagi, vases, and other sculptural fragments that adorned the Tivoli gardens, assigning them a monetary value and an asterisk if he felt they should enter the Louvre’s collection. He also inventoried hundreds of drawings in Boutin’s collection as well as paintings attributed to Vernet, Greuze, Poussin, Rubens, Teniers, and others. Vernet’s Bridge and its pendant were itemized as no. 39 on a list of 49 paintings taken from the rue de Richelieu, valued together at 3,600 livres. Although Le Brun did not give them an asterisk, they were in the Louvre’s collection by 1798 and remain there still.
provenanceEvents.imageSource: Inventory by Le Brun, Fragonard, and Bonvoisin of artworks seized from Boutin’s Tivoli residence, 1794. Archives nationales de France, F/7/1267.
provenanceEvents.imageAlt: Inventory of artworks seized from Boutin’s Tivoli residence, 1794.
